1.pericope_label: Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field; and he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?

schools.summary: Gill weighs the received rendering before he accepts it. Many instances are given of the subtlety of serpents — hiding their heads when struck at, rolling themselves up, stopping the ear at the voice of the charmer, putting off the skin, lying in sand of their own colour, biting the feet of horses — but by these it does not appear to be more subtle than any other creature, whatever it may have been at its first creation; particularly the fox greatly exceeds it. The words may therefore be rendered "that serpent," the particular serpent of which so much is spoken afterwards, or "the serpent was become," or "was made more subtle," that is, not naturally, but through Satan being in it and using it in a very subtle manner to answer his purposes and gain his point. A real serpent, and not the mere form or appearance of one, is meant, as is clear both from the account and from the curse afterwards pronounced on it; yet not that only, but as possessed and used by Satan. Calvin comes at the same question from the side of the tempter. The innate subtlety of the serpent did not prevent Satan from making use of the animal for effecting the destruction of man; since he required an instrument, he chose from among the animals the one he saw would be most suitable, and carefully contrived the method by which the snares he was preparing might the more easily take the mind of Eve by surprise. Hitherto he had held no communication with men, and therefore clothed himself with the person of an animal, under which he might open for himself the way of access. On the adjective, Calvin notes that interpreters do not agree in what sense the serpent is called subtil, some taking it in a good and others in a bad sense; he judges that Moses does not so much point out a fault as attribute praise to nature, because God had endued the beast with singular skill, which Satan then perverted to his own deceitful purposes. To the objection that more acuteness is now found in other animals, he answers that there would be nothing absurd in saying the gift so destructive to the human race was afterwards withdrawn. As for the silence about Satan, nothing more can be collected from this place than that men were deceived by the serpent; but the testimonies of Scripture are numerous in which the serpent is only the mouth of the devil, and Calvin subscribes to the opinion that the Holy Spirit then purposely used obscure figures, because full and clear light was reserved for the kingdom of Christ.

Henry is certain of the tempter's identity. It was the devil that beguiled Eve; the devil and Satan is that old serpent, a malignant spirit, by creation an angel of light and an immediate attendant upon God’s throne, but by sin become an apostate from his first state and a rebel against God’s crown and dignity. Multitudes of the angels fell, but this that attacked our first parents was surely the prince of the devils, the ring-leader in the rebellion: no sooner was he a sinner than he was a Satan, no sooner a traitor than a tempter, as one enraged against God and his glory and envious of man and his happiness. He knew he could not destroy man but by debauching him; the game he had to play was to draw our first parents to sin, and so to separate between them and their God. Thus the devil was, from the beginning, a murderer and the great mischief-maker, and the whole race of mankind had here, as it were, but one neck, and at that Satan struck. Whether it was only the visible shape and appearance of a serpent, or a real living serpent actuated and possessed by the devil, Henry leaves open; by God’s permission it might be either. Two reasons are given for the choice of creature: it is a specious creature, with a spotted dappled skin, and then went erect — perhaps a flying serpent, seeming to come from on high as a messenger from the upper world; and it is a subtle creature, which is what the verse itself notices. This serpent, as actuated by the devil, was no doubt more subtle than any other, for the devil, though he has lost the sanctity, retains the sagacity of an angel, and is wise to do evil. There is nothing by which the devil serves himself and his own interest more than by unsanctified subtlety. Henry adds that what Eve thought of a speaking serpent we are not likely to tell, since he believes she herself did not know what to think of it: at first she may have supposed it a good angel, and only afterwards suspected something amiss.

Clarke calls this one of the most difficult as well as the most important narratives in the whole book of God. The preceding chapter ended with the perfection and felicity of the first human beings, and this opens with their transgression and ruin; that man is in a fallen state the history of the world establishes beyond successful contradiction, but how, and by what agency, is a great mystery. Believing the account to be a simple relation of facts capable of a satisfactory explanation, he takes it up on that ground, and asks who the agent was. The word translated serpent is nachash, which he says has three meanings in Scripture: to view or observe attentively, and so to acquire knowledge by experience; brass or brazen, rendered in the English Bible by chains, fetters and even steel; and a serpent, though of what kind is nowhere determined. He surveys the places where the word occurs and finds it a general term confined to no one sense, so that neither the Septuagint nor the versions made from it can settle the matter. Turning to Arabic for its likeness to Hebrew, he finds a root meaning he departed, drew off, lay hid, seduced, from which come words for a creature of the ape kind, and also a name of the Devil, as the inspirer of evil and seducer from God and truth. From the account he draws five marks of the creature: that it stood at the head of the inferior animals for wisdom, that it walked erect, that it was endued with speech, that it was endued with reason, and that these were common to it, since the woman shows no surprise when it accosts her. Wesley, more briefly, has the devil in the shape of a serpent, chosen because it is a subtle creature, and thinks it not improbable that reason and speech were then the known properties of the serpent, which is why Eve was not surprised at his reasoning and speaking, as otherwise she must have been.

Ellicott begins with the particle and the wordplay. The verse opens with a simple "and," but the Hebrew language is very poor in particles, and the intended contrast would be made plainer by rendering "now they were both naked (arumim) . . . but the serpent was subtil (arum), more than every beast of the field." This quality of the serpent was in itself innocent, and even admirable, and accordingly the Septuagint translates it prudent; it was the tempter who made use of it to deceive Eve, and it has been remarked that she would not be surprised at finding herself spoken to by so sagacious a creature. If that is so, Ellicott adds, it follows that Eve must have dwelt in Paradise long enough to have learnt something of the habits of the animals around her, though she had never studied them so earnestly as Adam. On the address to the woman he holds that the leading point of the narrative is that the temptation came upon man from without, and through the woman; such questions, therefore, as whether it were a real serpent or Satan under a serpent-like form, whether it spake with a real voice, and whether the narrative describes a literal occurrence or is allegorical, are better left unanswered, the more reverent course being to draw the lessons the account was evidently intended to teach. In the opening question he hears a tone of surprise, as if the tempter could not bring himself to believe such a command had been given, and he marks that neither the serpent nor the woman uses the title Jehovah-Elohim common throughout this section — it is the impersonal God of creation to whom the tempter refers, and the woman follows his guidance, forgetting that it was Jehovah, the loving personal Being in covenant with them, who had really given the command. Keil and Delitzsch set the temptation against the completeness of what man already possessed: food in the fruit of the trees, a field of labour in the care of the garden, a capacious region for the expansion of his intellect in the animal and vegetable kingdoms, a positive law for the training of his moral nature in the tree of knowledge, and in the woman a suitable companion and help; and it was from the midst of the animal world that the tempter approached him.

2.pericope_label: The woman answers the serpent, and the serpent contradicts the threatening: Ye shall not surely die, for God doth know that ye shall be as gods

schools.summary: Gill reads the woman's reply with some charity. She answered him that spoke in the serpent, whom she might take to be a messenger from heaven, a holy angel; had she known who it was, she might be chargeable with imprudence in giving an answer and carrying on a conversation with him, and yet even supposing this, her answer may have had a good design — partly to set the matter in a true light and assert what was truth, and partly to set forth the goodness and liberality of God in the large provision he had made and the generous grant he had given them. From this discourse of Eve and the serpent, Gill adds, Plato no doubt had his notion of the first men discoursing with beasts. Of the tree he observes that it stood near the tree of life, and that she gives it no name, which perhaps had not yet been given; its name in the preceding chapter is written by anticipation, and most likely it had its name from the event. On the serpent's answer at the fifth verse Gill hears the insinuation plainly: God, who knows all things and foreknows all future events, knows that the effect of eating would be a clearer understanding and a greater degree of knowledge, which he is unwilling should be enjoyed, and has therefore endeavoured to prevent it by this prohibition — suggesting hatred in God of the creatures he had made, and an unwillingness that they should be as happy as they might. Calvin marks the change in the tempter's manner. Satan now springs more boldly forward, and because he sees a breach open before him he breaks through in a direct assault; he is never wont to engage in open war until we voluntarily expose ourselves to him, naked and unarmed, but approaches cautiously at first with blandishments, and when he has stolen in he dares to exalt himself petulantly and with proud confidence against God. Seizing upon Eve's doubt he penetrates further, that he may turn it into a direct negative: he no longer asks doubtingly whether the command be true, but openly accuses God of falsehood. Fatal temptation, Calvin exclaims, when while God is threatening us with death we not only securely sleep, but hold God himself in derision. He examines the several readings of the promise, prefers the singular sense, and concludes that Satan censures God as being moved by jealousy, and as having given the command for the purpose of keeping man in an inferior rank; Eve erred in not regulating the measure of her knowledge by the will of God, and we all daily suffer under the same disease, whereas the principal point of wisdom is a well-regulated sobriety in obedience to God.

Clarke asks whether the woman added something to what God had spoken. Did she not add "neither shall ye touch it"? Some of the Jewish writers, who are only serious on comparative trifles, state that as soon as she had asserted this the serpent pushed her against the tree and said, See, thou hast touched it, and art still alive; thou mayest therefore safely eat of the fruit, for surely thou shalt not die. At the flat denial he finds the tempter unmasked: here the father of lies at once appears, and appears too in flatly contradicting the assertion of God, insinuating through the nachash the impossibility of her dying — as if he had said, God has created thee immortal, thy death therefore is impossible, and God knows this, for as thou livest by the tree of life, so shalt thou get increase of wisdom by the tree of knowledge. On the promise of the fifth verse Clarke presses the translation. Your eyes shall be opened means your understanding shall be greatly enlightened and improved; and the word rendered "gods" should be translated "like God," since what idea could our first parents have had of gods before idolatry could have had any being, sin not having yet entered the world? The Syriac has the word in the singular and is the only one of all the versions which has hit on the true meaning. As the original word is the same which is used to point out the Supreme Being at the opening of the book, it has here the same signification, and the object of the tempter appears to have been to persuade our first parents that by eating of this fruit they should become wise and powerful as God — for knowledge is power — and be able to exist for ever, independently of him.

Ellicott takes the promise in its narrowest and therefore its strongest sense. Rather than "as gods," the phrase means as God, as Elohim himself, in the particular quality of knowing good and evil. It was a high bait which the tempter offered; and Eve, who at first had answered rightly, and who as yet knew nothing of falsehood, dallied with the temptation, and was lost. But we must not comment too severely upon her conduct, for it was no mean desire which led her astray: she longed for more knowledge and greater perfection, and wished even to rise above the level of her nature; the fault lay in the means, which were in violation of God's command, and so she fell. And, as usual, the tempter kept the promise to the ear. Eve did know good and evil, but only by feeling evil within herself; it was by moral degradation, and not by intellectual insight, that her ambitious wish was fulfilled.

6.pericope_label: The woman saw that the tree was good for food, and pleasant to the eyes, and took of the fruit, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband

schools.summary: Henry sets out first the inducements and then the steps. The woman, being deceived by the tempter's artful management, was ringleader in the transgression, and it was the result of her consideration, or rather her inconsideration. She saw no harm in this tree more than in any of the rest: it was said of all the fruit-trees of Eden that they were pleasant to the sight and good for food, and in her eye this was like all the rest, so that when there is thought to be no more harm in forbidden fruit than in other fruit, sin lies at the door and Satan soon carries the day. Perhaps it seemed to her better for food and more pleasant than any; or, having nothing in it more inviting than the rest, it was the more coveted because it was prohibited — for in our corrupt nature there dwells a strange spirit of contradiction, and we desire what is forbidden. She imagined more virtue in it than in any of the rest, a tree not only not to be dreaded but to be desired to make one wise; and this she perceived by what the devil had said, some thinking she saw the serpent eat of it and reasoned that if it made a brute creature rational, it might make a rational creature divine. Then follow the steps, not steps upward but downward towards the pit. She saw: a great deal of sin comes in at the eyes, and at those windows Satan throws in the fiery darts which pierce and poison the heart. She took: it was her own act and deed, for the devil did not put it into her mouth whether she would or no; Satan may tempt, but he cannot force. She did eat: perhaps she did not intend, when she looked, to take, nor when she took, to eat, but this was the result — the way of sin is downhill, and a man cannot stop himself when he will. She gave also to her husband: those that have themselves done ill are commonly willing to draw in others, and as was the devil, so was Eve, no sooner a sinner than a tempter. And he did eat, overcome by his wife's importunity — an act which involved disbelief of God's word together with confidence in the devil's, discontent with his present state, pride in his own merits, ambition of the honour that comes not from God, envy at God's perfections, and indulgence of the appetites of the body; in one word, disobedience to a plain, easy and express command which he knew to be a command of trial.

Gill keeps close to what the woman saw. Being near the tree, and perhaps just at it when the serpent first attacked her, she looked the more wishfully at it, and could discern nothing in the fruit which showed it to be bad and unfit to be eaten, or why it should be forbidden for food; on the contrary, it had a most promising aspect, as delicious, nourishing and salutary as any other fruit in the garden. Calvin looks behind the eye to the heart. This impure look of Eve, infected with the poison of concupiscence, was both the messenger and the witness of an impure heart. She could previously behold the tree with such sincerity that no desire to eat of it affected her mind, for the faith she had in the word of God was the best guardian of her heart and of all her senses; but now, after the heart had declined from faith and from obedience to the word, she corrupted both herself and all her senses, and depravity was diffused through all parts of her soul as well as her body. It is therefore a sign of impious defection that the woman now judges the tree to be good for food, delights herself in beholding it, and persuades herself that it is desirable for acquiring wisdom, whereas before she had passed by it a hundred times with an unmoved and tranquil look. Calvin also weighs whether Adam was present at the temptation, which he thinks by no means credible, though he allows that Adam may soon have joined her and been entangled by the same fallacies. On the nature of the sin he rejects as puerile the opinion of some of the ancients that they were allured by intemperance of appetite, since where there was such an abundance of the choicest fruits there could be no daintiness about one particular kind. Augustine is more correct, that pride was the beginning of all evils; but a fuller definition may be drawn from the kind of temptation Moses describes. First the woman is led away from the word of God by the wiles of Satan, through unbelief; so unbelief was the root of defection, just as faith alone unites us to God. Hence flowed ambition and pride, so that the woman first and then her husband desired to exalt themselves against God. In short, unbelief opened the door to ambition, and ambition proved the parent of rebellion.

Clarke counts three inducements and finds them the pattern of all temptation since. The fruit appeared wholesome and nutritive; its beauty tended to whet and increase appetite; and the promise of wisdom was an additional motive. From these three sources all natural and moral evil sprang, and they are exactly what the apostle calls the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eye, and the pride of life. Clarke will not have it that Adam was created so perfect as to preclude any increase in knowledge; on the contrary, our first parents were endued with a vast capacity to obtain knowledge, had all the means of information within their reach, met no hindrance to the direct conception of occurring truth, had every object of knowledge at hand, and possessed both the strongest propensity to know and the greatest pleasure in knowing. That state of perfection is precisely what makes the transgression intelligible: it was natural for them to desire to be increasingly wise, since God had implanted the desire; but he showed them that it should be gratified in a certain way, that prudence and judgment should regulate it, and that they should not pry into what he chose to conceal. There is a rule for all things, and fixed limits on either side of which righteousness cannot be found; God assigned the limits, and assigned the means also. Wesley follows Henry's account of the inducements and the steps, and marks in particular that it is likely Adam was not with her when she was tempted — surely if he had been, he would have interposed to prevent the sin — but that he came to her when she had eaten and was prevailed upon by her to eat likewise; she persuaded him with the same arguments the serpent had used with her, adding that she herself had eaten of it and found it so far from being deadly that it was extremely pleasant.

Ellicott would keep the Hebrew form of the sentence, which our version has smoothed away: "And the woman saw . . . and she took," in which the progress of the temptation is detailed in a far more lively manner. With awakened desire the woman gazes upon the tree; the fruit appears inviting to the eye, and possibly was really good for food; the whole aspect of the tree was beautiful; and besides all this there was the promise held out to her that it possessed the mysterious faculty of developing her intellectual powers. To this combined influence of her senses without and her ambition within she was unable to offer that resistance which would have been possible only by a living faith in the spoken word of God. She eats, therefore, and gives to her husband — so called here for the first time — and he eats with her. The demeanour of Adam throughout Ellicott finds extraordinary. It is the woman who is tempted, and not as though Adam were absent, as Milton supposes, for she has not to seek him; he shares with her at once the gathered fruit. She is pictured as more quick and observant, more open to impressions, more curious and full of longings than the man, whose passive behaviour is as striking as the woman's eagerness and excitability.

7.pericope_label: The eyes of them both were opened; they sewed fig leaves together, and hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees

schools.summary: Gill insists that the opening of the eyes was of the mind and not of the body, and that what it disclosed was not the advance promised but things very disagreeable and distressing. Their eyes were opened to see that they had been deceived by the serpent, that they had broken the commandment of God, and incurred the displeasure of their Creator and kind benefactor, and had brought ruin and destruction upon themselves; they saw what blessings and privileges they had lost — communion with God, the dominion of the creatures, the purity and holiness of their nature — and what miseries they had involved themselves and their posterity in, how exposed they now were to the wrath of God, the curse of the law, and eternal death. At the sound of the voice in the garden Gill notes that they had heard it before and knew it, though perhaps now in another tone and very terrible, which before was mild and gentle, pleasant and delightful. Some understand by it a clap of thunder, sometimes called the voice of the Lord, and the rather because a wind is mentioned afterwards; but Gill takes it rather of the voice of the Son of God, the eternal Word, appearing in human form as a pledge of his future incarnation, and that not only as a Judge to arraign and condemn, but as a Saviour of men, so that they had no reason to entertain such terrible apprehensions of him as to flee from him; and he cites the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan, which paraphrase it "the voice of the Word of the Lord God." Calvin observes that it was necessary that the eyes of Eve should be veiled till her husband also was deceived, and that now both, alike bound by the chain of an unhappy consent, begin to be sensible of their wretchedness, though not yet affected with a deep knowledge of their fault. They are ashamed of their nakedness, and yet, though convinced, they do not humble themselves before God nor fear his judgments as they ought, but resort to evasions. Some progress there is: whereas recently they would, like giants, assault heaven by storm, now, confounded with a sense of their own ignominy, they flee to hiding-places. This spontaneous shame Calvin takes for a sure token of guilt, since they are not yet summoned to the tribunal of God and there is none who accuses them, so that their own conscience has become the judge which compels them to confess their fault. Of the girdles he asks for what end they were made, and answers, that they might keep God at a distance as by an invincible barrier: there is none of us who does not smile at their folly, and yet we are all infected with the same disease, resorting to vain trifles as if it were an easy thing to delude God. As soon as the voice of God sounds, the leaves by which they thought themselves well protected are of no avail; all bury the disgrace of their vices under flimsy leaves till God by his voice strikes inwardly upon their consciences, and he who had found a few leaves unavailing fled to whole trees.

Clarke reviews the whole transaction at this point and then measures its effects. Satan associated himself with the creature in order to seduce and ruin mankind; knowing that while they depended on God they could not be ruined, he endeavoured to seduce them from that dependence, working on the mind's proper desire for an increase of knowledge, insinuating that the prohibition came from envy, and persuading them that they could not fall from their present blessedness — a temptation by which he has ever since fatally succeeded in the ruin of multitudes, persuading them that being once right they could never finally go wrong. The effects follow. Their eyes were opened, and they saw what they never saw before: that they were stripped of their excellence, had lost their innocence, and had fallen into a state of indigence and danger. Yet though their eyes were opened to see their nakedness, their mind was clouded and their judgment confused; they seem to have lost all just notions of honour and dishonour, since it was shameful to break the commandment of God, and neither shameful nor dishonourable to go naked when clothing was not necessary. They seem in a moment to have lost not only sound judgment but reflection: a short time before, Adam was so wise that he could name all the creatures according to their respective natures and qualities, and could tell at once what Eve was and for what end she was made, though he had been in a deep sleep when God formed her; now he does not know the first principle concerning the divine nature, that it knows all things and is omnipresent, and therefore endeavours to hide himself among the trees from the eye of the all-seeing God. Clarke adds that this account could never have been credited had not its proofs been continued by uninterrupted succession to the present time, since every human being still endeavours to obtain knowledge by unlawful means, still seeks to be independent and to live without God in the world, and still seeks privacy for his crimes, solicitous only to hide them from the eye of man. On the visit itself he thinks God used to converse with our first parents in the garden, and that the usual time was the decline of the day, in the evening breeze; probably this was the time employed in the more solemn acts of religious worship. The time for that worship is come again, and God is in his place; but Adam and Eve have sinned, and instead of being found in the place of worship are hidden among the trees.

Ellicott dates the consciousness of guilt to the moment of the act, and argues from it that they ate together, since otherwise Eve would have been guilty of leading Adam into sin after her own understanding had been enlightened to perceive the consequences; manifestly her deed was not without his cognisance and approval, and he had shared, in his own way, her ambition of attaining to the Godlike. How miserably the proud desire was disappointed: their increased knowledge brought only shame, their minds were awakened and enlarged, but the price they paid for it was their innocence and peace. On the leaves he sees no reason for supposing them those of the pisang, which grow ten feet long, since everywhere else the word signifies the common fig-tree, one of the earliest plants subjected to man's use; and he finds the verb "sewed" more remarkable, the Syriac translator, feeling the difficulty of supposing Eve acquainted with needlework, rendering it that they stuck leaves together. The word implies something more elaborate, and Ellicott conjectures that some time elapsed between the sin and its punishment, allowing not merely a first hasty covering but something more careful and ingenious; the word rendered aprons he would render girdles. On the eighth verse he sets aside the matter-of-fact school who understand a thunderstorm, and reads the verb as reflexive: Jehovah appears as the owner of the Paradise, taking in it his daily exercise, walking for pleasure at the hour when the evening breeze sets in and men rise from their noontide slumber. The primary lesson is that hitherto man had lived in close communication with God — the nobler side of Adam's relationship before the fall. In their hiding he sees an attempt to escape a further result of sin: the first result was shame, from which man endeavoured to free himself by covering his person; the second was fear, and this man would cure by departing still farther from God. But the voice of Jehovah reaches him, and with rebuke and punishment gives also healing and hope. Keil and Delitzsch name what was lost as that blessed blindness, the ignorance of innocence, which knows nothing of nakedness; the discovery excited shame, which they sought to conceal by an outward covering. The word always denotes the fig-tree, not the pisang or the Indian banana, whose leaves are twelve feet long and two feet broad, for there would have been no necessity to sew those together at all; and what they made were aprons worn round the hips. The need of covering arose not because the fruit had poisoned the fountain of human life or corrupted the body by some inherent quality, nor because any physical change ensued, but from the destruction of the innocence in which they had stood.

9.pericope_label: And the LORD God called unto Adam, Where art thou? And he said, I heard thy voice, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself

schools.summary: Henry treats the question as the opening of a trial: here is the arraignment of these deserters before the righteous Judge of heaven and earth, who, though he is not tied to observe formalities, yet proceeds against them with all possible fairness, that he may be justified when he speaks. The question is startling and arresting — not as if God did not know where he was, but thus he would enter the process against him. Some make it a bemoaning question, poor Adam, what has become of thee, alas for thee, how art thou fallen; Henry takes it rather as upbraiding, in order to conviction and humiliation: not in what place, but in what condition. Is this all thou hast gotten by eating forbidden fruit? Thou that wouldest vie with me, dost thou now fly from me? From this he draws two notes. Those who by sin have gone astray from God should seriously consider where they are: they are afar off from all good, in the midst of their enemies, in bondage to Satan, and in the high road to utter ruin. And this enquiry after Adam may be looked upon as a gracious pursuit, in kindness to him and in order to his recovery — had God not called to him to reclaim him, his condition would have been as desperate as that of the fallen angels, and this lost sheep would have wandered endlessly if the good Shepherd had not sought after him. If sinners will but consider where they are, they will not rest till they return to God. Of the answer Henry observes that Adam does not own his guilt, and yet in effect confesses it by owning his shame and fear; it is the common fault and folly of those that have done an ill thing, when questioned about it, to acknowledge no more than what is so manifest that they cannot deny it. He was afraid because he was naked: not only unarmed, and therefore afraid to contend with God, but unclothed, and therefore afraid so much as to appear before him. We have reason to be afraid of approaching to God if we be not clothed and fenced with the righteousness of Christ, for nothing but this will be armour of proof and cover the shame of our nakedness.

Gill notes who called and who answered. The Jerusalem Targum has here the Word of the Lord God, the second Person, and this, Gill says, is the voice Adam is said to have heard before; and in the answer, "I heard thy voice in the garden," the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan again have the voice of thy Word. But this, he adds, was not the true cause of Adam's hiding himself, for he had heard that voice in the garden before, when it did not strike him with terror but gave him pleasure. Calvin asks why a second call was needed. They had already been smitten by the voice of God, but lay confounded under the trees until another voice more effectually penetrated their minds; the former was a confused sound which had no sufficient force to press upon the conscience, and therefore God now approaches nearer, and from the tangled thicket of trees draws Adam, however unwilling and resisting, forth into the midst. In the same manner we also are alarmed at the voice of God as soon as his law sounds in our ears, but presently we snatch at shadows, until he, calling upon us more vehemently, compels us to come forward, arraigned at his tribunal. Paul calls this the life of the law, when it slays us by charging us with our sins; for as long as we are pleased with ourselves, and are inflated with a false notion that we are alive, the law is dead to us, because we blunt its point by our hardness, but when it pierces us more sharply we are driven into new terrors. Of the answer itself Calvin says that although it seems the confession of a dejected and humbled man, it will soon appear that he was not yet properly subdued nor led to repentance. He imputes his fear to the voice of God and to his own nakedness, as if he had never before heard God speaking without being alarmed, and had not been even sweetly exhilarated by his speech. His excessive stupidity appears in this, that he fails to recognise the cause of shame in his sin, and therefore shows that he does not yet so feel his punishment as to confess his fault; and he proves, notwithstanding his fig-leaves, that original sin does not reside in one part of the body only but holds its dominion over the whole man, since he still dreads the presence of God.

Keil and Delitzsch put the purpose of the question plainly: the man could not hide himself from God, and Jehovah God called unto Adam and said, Where art thou — not that he was ignorant of his hiding-place, but to bring him to a confession of his sin. When Adam answered that he had hidden himself through fear of his nakedness, he sought to hide the sin behind its consequences, his disobedience behind the feeling of shame; and this, they argue, is not to be regarded as a sign of peculiar obduracy, but admits easily of a psychological explanation — at the time he actually thought more of his nakedness and shame than of his transgression of the divine command, and his consciousness of the effects of his sin was keener than his sense of the sin itself. To awaken the latter God asked him who had told him that he was naked, and pressed on to the tree and the command.

Clarke sets down the two immediate consequences of sin as the answer itself displays them. First shame, because of the ingratitude marked in the rebellion, and because in aiming to be like God they were now sunk into a state of the greatest wretchedness; then fear, because they saw they had been deceived by Satan, and were exposed to that death and punishment from which he had promised them an exemption. How worthy is it of remark, he adds, that this cause continues to produce the very same effects: shame and fear were the first fruits of sin, and fruits which it has invariably produced, from the first transgression to the present time. Wesley reads the question as mercy rather than mere arraignment: this enquiry after Adam may be looked upon as a gracious pursuit, in order to his recovery, and if God had not called to him to reduce him, his condition had been as desperate as that of the fallen angels. Of the answer he keeps Henry's distinction, that Adam was afraid because he was naked — not only unarmed, and therefore afraid to contend with God, but unclothed, and therefore afraid so much as to appear before him.

11.pericope_label: Who told thee that thou wast naked? The man blames the woman and the woman blames the serpent: The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat

schools.summary: Henry sets the passage out as a confession extorted and then extenuated. God put the first question to the man, who told thee that thou wast naked, hast thou eaten of the forbidden tree; and Henry notes that though God knows all our sins, yet he will know them from us, and requires from us an ingenuous confession of them, not that he may be informed, but that we may be humbled. In the examination God reminds Adam of the command he had given — I commanded thee not to eat of it, I thy Maker, I thy Master, I thy benefactor — for sin appears most plain and most sinful in the glass of the commandment, and in it we should see our faces. The question put to the woman, what is this that thou hast done, Henry reads as a summons to consider the evil of the act: in eating forbidden fruit we have offended a great and gracious God, broken a just and righteous law, violated a sacred and most solemn covenant, and wronged our own precious souls; and in enticing others to eat of it we do the devil's work, make ourselves guilty of other men's sins, and accessory to their ruin. It was to no purpose to plead not guilty, for the show of their countenances testified against them, and so they became their own accusers; but these do not look like penitent confessions, since instead of aggravating the sin and taking shame to themselves, they excuse the sin and lay the shame and blame on others. Adam lays all the blame upon his wife: she gave it me, and pressed me to eat, which I did only to oblige her — a frivolous excuse, since he ought to have taught her, not to have been taught by her, and it was no hard matter to determine which of the two he must be ruled by, his God or his wife. Worse than this, he words it so as tacitly to reflect on God himself: it is the woman whom thou gavest me, and gavest to be with me, insinuating that God was accessory to his sin. There is a strange proneness in those that are tempted to say they are tempted of God, as if our abusing God's gifts would excuse our violation of God's laws. Eve in her turn lays all the blame upon the serpent, and Henry remarks that sin is a brat nobody is willing to own, a sign that it is a scandalous thing: those willing enough to take the pleasure and profit of sin are backward enough to take the blame and shame of it. From her plea he draws two lessons — that Satan's temptations are all beguilings, his arguments all fallacies and his allurements all cheats, so that when he speaks fair we should not believe him; and that though his subtlety drew us into sin, it will not justify us in sin, for though he is the tempter, we are the sinners.

Gill marks the reluctance in both answers. Adam speaks not being able any longer to conceal the truth, though he shifts off the blame as much as possible from himself; and the woman is addressed as the one who was first in the transgression, and drew her husband into it, and upon whom he seemingly casts the blame of his eating the forbidden fruit. Calvin reads the first question as an indirect reprimand meant to reprove the sottishness of Adam in not perceiving his fault in his punishment: it is not simply that Adam was afraid at the voice of God, but that the voice of his judge was formidable to him because he was a sinner; and it was not his nakedness but the turpitude of the vice with which he had defiled himself that was the cause of fear. He was guilty of intolerable impiety against God in seeking the origin of evil in nature — not that he would accuse God in express terms, but, deploring his own misery and dissembling the fact that he was himself the author of it, he malignantly transfers to God the charge which he ought to have brought against himself. God asks in the language of doubt, not as searching into some disputable matter, but for the purpose of piercing more acutely the stupid man who, labouring under a fatal disease, is yet unconscious of his malady, just as a sick man who complains that he is burning yet thinks not of fever; and the clause about the command is added to remove the pretext of ignorance, since Adam was admonished in time and fell from no other cause than that he knowingly and voluntarily brought destruction upon himself. At the twelfth verse Calvin sees the boldness of Adam more clearly betray itself: so far from being subdued, he breaks forth into coarser blasphemy, having before been tacitly expostulating with God and now beginning to contend with him. Just as if conscious of no evil, he puts his wife as the guilty party in his place, and not content with this brings an accusation against God at the same time, objecting that the wife who had brought ruin upon him had been given by God. We also, trained in the same school of original sin, are too ready to resort to subterfuges of the same kind, but to no purpose; for howsoever instigations from other quarters may impel us, the unbelief which seduces us from obedience to God is within us, and the pride is within which brings forth contempt. Turning to the woman, Calvin says God contends no further with the man, since he aggravates rather than diminishes his crime, and though he rages he is yet held convicted. The Hebrew phrase addressed to the woman has more vehemence than the old interpreter allowed: rather than why hast thou done this, it should be rendered how hast thou done this, the language of one who wonders as at something prodigious. Eve ought to have been confounded at the portentous wickedness of which she was admonished, yet she is not struck dumb, but after the example of her husband transfers the charge to another, and by laying the blame on the serpent foolishly and impiously thinks herself absolved. But who compelled Eve to listen to his fallacies, and even to place confidence in them more readily than in the word of God?

Clarke finds in these answers further proofs of the fallen state of man, and proofs that its consequences extend to his remotest posterity. On the question whether he had eaten of the tree, Adam is obliged to acknowledge his transgression, but does it in such a way as to shift the blame from himself and lay it upon God and upon the woman: this woman whom thou didst give to be my companion, she gave me, and I did eat — I have no further blame in this transgression, I did not pluck the fruit, she took it and gave it to me. When the woman is questioned she lays the blame upon God and the serpent: thou didst make him much wiser than thou didst make me, and therefore my simplicity and ignorance were overcome by his superior wisdom and subtlety; the fault is his, and his who made him so wise and me so ignorant. Thus, Clarke concludes, while the eyes of their body were opened to see their degraded state, the eyes of their understanding were closed, so that they could not see the sinfulness of sin, and at the same time their hearts were hardened through its deceitfulness. In this also their posterity copy their example, for how few ingenuously confess their own sin: the strength and subtlety of the tempter, the natural weakness of their own minds, the unfavourable circumstances in which they were placed, are all pleaded as excuses, and thus the possibility of repentance is precluded, since till a man take his sin to himself, till he acknowledge that he alone is guilty, he cannot be humbled, and consequently cannot be saved. Wesley sums the hearing up more briefly: neither of them will own the fault fully, Adam laying all the blame upon his wife and tacitly upon God himself, and Eve laying all upon the serpent; and the prisoners being found guilty by their own confession, besides the infallible knowledge of the Judge, and nothing material being offered in arrest of judgment, God proceeds immediately to pass sentence.

Ellicott reads the question about the nakedness as the turning of Adam's mind from the symptom to the disease. Adam had given as his excuse that which was really the consequence of his sin; but by this question God awakens his conscience, and makes him feel that what he had described as a want or imperfection was really the result of his own act. And as long as a man feels sorrow only for the results of his actions there is no repentance, and no wish to return to the Divine presence. God, therefore, in order to win Adam back to better thoughts, carries his mind from the effect to the sin that had caused it.

14.pericope_label: Because thou hast done this, thou art cursed above all cattle; upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life

schools.summary: Henry explains why sentence falls on the serpent without any examination. The prisoners being found guilty by their own confession, besides the personal and infallible knowledge of the Judge, and nothing material being offered in arrest of judgment, God proceeds to pass sentence, and begins where the sin began. He did not examine the serpent, nor ask him what he had done nor why he did it, but immediately sentenced him: because he was already convicted of rebellion against God, his malice and wickedness notorious, not found by secret search but openly avowed and declared as Sodom's; and because he was to be for ever excluded from all hope of pardon — why should anything be said to convince and humble him who was to find no place for repentance? His wound was not searched, because it was not to be cured. Henry then divides the sentence. Taken as lighting upon the serpent, the brute creature which Satan made use of, it testifies God's displeasure against sin and his jealousy for the injured honour of Adam and Eve: the creature was made, like the rest, for the service of man, and was now abused to his hurt, and therefore God fastens a curse and reproach upon it and makes it to groan, being burdened. The devil's instruments must share in the devil's punishments; thus the bodies of the wicked, though only instruments of unrighteousness, shall partake of everlasting torments with the soul, and even the ox that killed a man must be stoned. See here, Henry says, how God hates sin, and especially how much displeased he is with those who entice others into sin. The serpent is laid under the curse of God: even the creeping things, when God made them, were blessed of him, but sin turned the blessing into a curse, and the creature that was more subtle than any beast of the field is here cursed above every beast of the field. Unsanctified subtlety often proves a great curse to a man, and the more crafty men are to do evil the more mischief they do; subtle tempters are the most accursed creatures under the sun. He is laid also under man's reproach: upon thy belly thou shalt go, no longer upon feet or half erect, but crawling along, thy belly cleaving to the earth, an expression of a very abject and miserable condition; and thou shalt not avoid eating dust with thy meat. His crime was that he tempted Eve to eat that which she should not; his punishment was that he was necessitated to eat that which he would not. This denotes not only a base and despicable condition, but a mean and pitiful spirit, for it is said of those whose courage has departed from them that they lick the dust like a serpent; and how sad it is that the serpent's curse should be the covetous worldling's choice, whose character it is that he pants after the dust of the earth.

Gill applies the sentence to both the serpent and the devil in it: literally to the serpent, and mystically to Satan. Both are punished, and that very justly — the serpent as the instrument Satan made use of, cursed for his sake as the earth was for man's; and the punishing of the instrument as well as the principal the more discovers God's detestation of the act for which they are punished. Nor could it have been agreeable to the justice of God to punish the instrument and let the principal go free, and therefore the whole sentence must be considered as respecting them both. Gill observes further that no pains are taken to convince Satan of his sin, nor any time spent in reasoning and debating with him about it, he being a hardened apostate spirit, doomed to everlasting destruction, and without any hope of mercy and forgiveness; what follows is said to show the divine resentment of his crime. Calvin gives the same reason from the other side: God does not interrogate the serpent as he had done the man and the woman, because in the animal itself there was no sense of sin, and because to the devil he would hold out no hope of pardon. He might truly, by his own authority, have pronounced sentence against Adam and Eve unheard; why then does he call them to undergo examination, except that he has a care for their salvation? There would be no need of any trial of the cause, or of any solemn form of judgment, in order to condemn us; wherefore, while God insists upon extorting a confession from us, he acts rather as a physician than as a judge. On the doubt whether the words refer to the serpent or to the devil, Calvin holds that the language is of a mixed character, God so addressing the serpent that the last clause belongs to the devil. If it seem absurd that the punishment of another's fraud should be exacted from a brute animal, the solution is at hand: since the creature had been made for the benefit of man, there was nothing improper in its being accursed from the moment it was employed for his destruction, and by this act of vengeance God would prove how highly he estimates the salvation of man, just as if a father should hold in execration the sword by which his son had been slain. As to the objection that creeping and eating dust are the serpent's nature, Calvin answers that there is no absurdity in supposing it was again consigned to that former condition to which it was already naturally subject — thrust back into its proper rank, as if it had been said, thou, a wretched and filthy animal fixed to the earth, hast dared to rise up against man, and I now throw thee back again to the place whence thou hast attempted to emerge. To eat dust is the sign of a vile and sordid nature, and Isaiah confirms the sense when, promising under the reign of Christ the complete restoration of nature, he records that dust shall be to the serpent for bread.

Clarke divides the sentence in two, one falling on Satan and the other on the agent he employed. The tempter is not asked why he deceived the woman, for he cannot roll the blame on any other: self-tempted he fell, and it is natural for him, such is his enmity, to deceive and destroy all he can; his fault admits of no excuse, and therefore God begins to pronounce sentence on him first. The nachash, whom Clarke supposes to have stood at the head of all the inferior animals and in a sort of society and intimacy with man, is to be greatly degraded, entirely banished from human society, and deprived of the gift of speech. Cursed above all cattle means that it shall be considered the most contemptible of animals; upon thy belly shalt thou go, that it shall no longer walk erect, but mark the ground equally with its hands and feet; and dust shalt thou eat, that though formerly possessed of the faculty to distinguish, choose and cleanse its food, it shall henceforth feed like the most stupid and abject quadruped, and that through all the innumerable generations of its species. God saw meet to manifest his displeasure against the agent employed in this melancholy business, and Clarke thinks this founded on the part the intelligent and subtle creature took in the seduction of our first parents, since we see that he was capable of it and have some reason to believe that he became a willing instrument. Wesley keeps to the reversal in the curse: to testify his displeasure against sin God fastens a curse upon the serpent, and though even the creeping things when God made them were blessed of him, sin turned the blessing into a curse; upon thy belly shalt thou go, no longer upon feet or half erect, but crawling along, thy belly cleaving to the earth, and dust thou shalt eat, which signifies a base and despicable condition.

15.pericope_label: I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel

schools.summary: Gill measures the enmity against the familiarity it displaced. Between the woman and the serpent there had been much familiarity, not only in the discourse just held but before it; some conjecture that she took a particular liking to the creature and was delighted with it, laid it perhaps in her bosom, adorned her neck with its windings, or made it a bracelet for her arms, and that being a peculiar favourite the devil made choice of it as his instrument to deceive her. Being now beguiled by it she conceived an antipathy against it, and that antipathy has become natural between the serpent and man: man abhors the sight of a serpent, and the serpent the sight of man, and the spittle of a man and the gall of a serpent are poison to each other; the antipathy is observed to be stronger in the female sex. And this was true not only of the particular serpent that deceived Eve and of the particular woman deceived by him, but of every serpent and of every woman in successive ages, and is also true of Satan and the church of God in all ages. Calvin takes the first sense the same way: there should always be that hostile strife between the human race and serpents which is now apparent, for by a secret feeling of nature man abhors them, and it is regarded as among prodigies that some men take pleasure in them; as often as the sight of a serpent inspires us with horror, the memory of our fall is renewed. He joins the following clause to it in one continued discourse: there shall be such hatred that on both sides they shall be troublesome to each other, the serpent vexatious towards men and men intent on the destruction of serpents. Yet the Lord acts mercifully in chastising man, whom he does not suffer Satan to touch except in the heel, while he subjects the head of the serpent to be wounded by him; in the terms head and heel there is a distinction between the superior and the inferior, and thus God leaves some remains of dominion to man, so placing their mutual disposition to injure each other that their condition should not be equal, but man be superior in the conflict. From the serpent Calvin then makes a transition to the author of the mischief, for God has not so vented his anger upon the outward instrument as to spare the devil, with whom lay all the blame. It is worth observing, he says, that the Lord spoke not for the sake of the serpent but of the man — for what end could it answer to thunder against the serpent in unintelligible words? Respect was had to men, both that they might be affected with a greater dread of sin, seeing how highly displeasing it is to God, and that they might take consolation for their misery, perceiving that God is still propitious to them. Slender indeed would be the ground of hope if only a serpent were meant, since nothing would then be provided for except the fading life of the body, and men would remain the slaves of Satan. Wherefore, that God might revive the fainting minds of men, it became necessary to promise them, in their posterity, victory over Satan. Calvin corrects the Vulgate's feminine reading and rejects the profane exposition built upon it, which applies to the mother of Christ what is said concerning her seed; he takes the seed to mean the posterity of the woman generally, and since not all the sons of Adam arise as conquerors of the devil, comes necessarily to one head in whom the victory lies, remembering Paul's word that the Lord shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly, and that God crowns none but well-tried wrestlers.

Clarke disputes the popular reading of the enmity. It has generally been supposed to apply to a certain enmity subsisting between men and serpents, but this is rather a fancy than a reality: it is yet to be discovered that the serpentine race have any peculiar enmity against mankind, nor is there any proof that men hate serpents more than they do other noxious animals — men have much more enmity to the common rat and magpie, because the former destroy the grain, and serpents in general, far from seeking to do men mischief, flee man's approach and generally avoid his dwelling. If the word nachash be taken of a creature of the ape kind, he finds a more consistent meaning, since scarcely an animal in the universe is so detested by most women. But we are not to look for merely literal meanings here: it is evident that Satan, who actuated this creature, is alone intended in this part of the prophetic declaration, and God in his endless mercy has put enmity between men and him, so that though all mankind love his service, yet all invariably hate himself — were it otherwise, who could be saved? A great point gained towards the conversion of a sinner is to convince him that it is Satan he has been serving. Deeper still lies the promise, and Clarke presses the pronoun: it is He who shall bruise the head, the seed of the woman, the person to come by the woman and by her alone, without the concurrence of man. Therefore the address is not to Adam and Eve, but to Eve alone, and it was in consequence of this purpose of God that Jesus Christ was born of a virgin; this, and this alone, is what is implied in the promise of the seed of the woman bruising the head of the serpent. Christ died to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself, and to destroy him who had the power of death; thus he bruises his head, destroying his power and lordship over mankind and turning them from the power of Satan unto God. And Satan bruises his heel: God so ordered it that the salvation of man could only be brought about by the death of Christ, and even the spiritual seed of our blessed Lord have the heel often bruised, as they suffer persecution and temptation. Wesley numbers what the promise gives notice of concerning Christ: his incarnation, that he should be the seed of the woman; his sufferings and death, pointed at in Satan's bruising his heel, that is, his human nature; and his victory over Satan thereby. Satan had now trampled upon the woman and insulted over her, but the seed of the woman should be raised up in the fulness of time to avenge her quarrel, and to trample upon him, to spoil him, to lead him captive, and to triumph over him. Wesley also fastens the perpetual reproach upon the enemy under the cover of the serpent: degraded and accursed of God, since it is supposed that pride was the sin that turned angels into devils, and is here justly punished by mortifications couched under the mean circumstances of a serpent crawling on his belly and licking the dust; detested and abhorred of all mankind, since even those really seduced into his interest profess a hatred of him; and destroyed and ruined at last by the great Redeemer, signified by the bruising of his head, his subtle politics all baffled and his usurped power entirely crushed. It is the fruit of this enmity that there is a continual conflict between God's people and him, for heaven and hell can never be reconciled, no more can Satan and a sanctified soul; and a continual struggle between the wicked and the good, all the malice of persecutors against the people of God being the fruit of this enmity, which will continue while there is a godly man on this side heaven and a wicked man on this side hell.

16.pericope_label: Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee

schools.summary: Henry sets the sentence under two heads: the woman is condemned to a state of sorrow and to a state of subjection, proper punishments of a sin in which she had gratified her pleasure and her pride. Of the sorrow only one particular is specified, that in bringing forth children, but it includes all those impressions of grief and fear which the mind of that tender sex is most apt to receive, and all the common calamities they are liable to. Sin brought sorrow into the world; it was this that made the world a vale of tears, brought showers of trouble upon our heads and opened springs of sorrow in our hearts — had we known no guilt, we should have known no grief. The pains of child-bearing, great to a scripture proverb, are the effect of sin, and every pang and every groan of the travailing woman speaks aloud the fatal consequences of sin. Henry marks that the sorrows are multiplied, greatly multiplied: they include not only the travailing throes but the indispositions before, so that it is sorrow from the conception, and the nursing toils and vexations after; and if the children prove wicked and foolish they are, more than ever, the heaviness of her that bore them. He marks also whose hand does it: I will do it, says God, who as a righteous Judge does it, which ought to silence us under all our sorrows, since as many as they are we have deserved them all and more; and who as a tender Father does it for our necessary correction, that we may be humbled for sin and weaned from the world. Under the second head, the whole sex, which by creation was equal with man, is for sin made inferior, and the wife particularly is put under the dominion of her husband and is not at her own disposal. The sentence amounts only to the apostolic command that wives be in subjection to their own husbands, but the entrance of sin has made that duty a punishment which otherwise it would not have been: if man had not sinned he would always have ruled with wisdom and love, and if the woman had not sinned she would always have obeyed with humility and meekness, and then the dominion would have been no grievance — it is our own sin and folly that make our yoke heavy. Those wives who not only disobey their husbands but domineer over them do not consider that they violate a divine law and thwart a divine sentence. Finally Henry observes how mercy is mixed with wrath: the woman shall have sorrow, but it shall be in bringing forth children, and the sorrow shall be forgotten for joy that a child is born; she shall be subject, but to her own husband that loves her, not to a stranger or an enemy; the sentence was not a curse to bring her to ruin, but a chastisement to bring her to repentance, and it was well that enmity was not put between the man and the woman, as it was between the serpent and the woman.

Clarke renders the doubled Hebrew verb as multiplying I will multiply — I will multiply thy sorrows, and multiply those sorrows by other sorrows, and this during conception and pregnancy, and particularly so in child-bearing. This curse, he says, has fallen in a heavier degree on the woman than on any other female; nothing is better attested than this, and yet there is certainly no natural reason why it should be so: it is a part of her punishment, and a part from which even God's mercy will not exempt her. On the clause that follows he takes the desire as appetite, so that she shall not be able to shun the great pain and peril of child-bearing; and he presses the difficulty of the last clause honestly, observing that at their creation both were formed with equal rights, and the woman had probably as much right to rule as the man, but that subjection to the will of her husband is one part of her curse — and so very capricious is that will often, that a sorer punishment no human being can well have, who is at all in a state of liberty and under the protection of wise and equal laws. Wesley keeps Henry's two heads, that she is condemned to a state of sorrow and a state of subjection, proper punishments of a sin in which she had gratified her pleasure and her pride; and he presses in particular whose hand multiplies the sorrows: it is God that multiplies our sorrows, I will do it, God as a righteous Judge, which ought to silence us under all our sorrows, since as many as they are we have deserved them all and more, and God as a tender Father, for our necessary correction, that we may be humbled for sin and weaned from it.

Gill notes the order of the sentencing: the woman receives her sentence next to the serpent and before the man, because she was first and more deeply in the transgression, and was the means of drawing her husband into it. Calvin marks the brevity of the proceeding. In order that the majesty of the judge may shine the more brightly, God uses no long disputation, whence also we may perceive of what avail are all our tergiversations with him: in bringing the serpent forward Eve thought she had herself escaped, but God, disregarding her cavils, condemns her. Let the sinner therefore, when he comes to the bar of God, cease to contend, lest he more severely provoke against himself the anger of him whom he has already too highly offended. On the punishment itself Calvin takes the word to comprise all the trouble women sustain from the beginning of pregnancy — distaste for food, faintings, weariness, and innumerable other things — until they come to the birth, which brings the bitterest torments with it. It is credible, he says, that the woman would have brought forth without pain, or at least without such great suffering, if she had stood in her original condition, but her revolt from God subjected her to inconveniences of this kind; and the expression pains and conception is to be taken for the pains which they endure in consequence of conception. The second punishment he calls subjection, for the form of speech that her desire shall be unto her husband is of the same force as if God had said that she should not be free and at her own command, but subject to the authority of her husband and dependent upon his will. Thus the woman, who had perversely exceeded her proper bounds, is forced back to her own position: she had indeed previously been subject to her husband, but that was a liberal and gentle subjection, whereas now she is cast into servitude.

Ellicott insists on the difference between this sentence and the serpent's: the woman is not cursed as the serpent was, but punished as next in guilt, and the retribution is twofold. First God greatly multiplies her sorrow and her conception — that is, her sorrow generally, but especially in connection with pregnancy, when with anguish and peril of life she wins the joy of bringing a man into the world. Then her desire shall be to her husband: in the sin she had been the prime actor, and the man had yielded her too ready an obedience, and henceforward she was to live in subjection to him; yet not unhappy, because her inferiority was to be tempered by a natural longing for the married state and by love towards her master. Ellicott traces what became of this in history. Among the heathen the punishment was made very bitter by the degradation to which woman was reduced; among the Jews the wife, though she never sank so low, was nevertheless purchased of her father, was liable to divorce at the husband's will, and was treated as in all respects his inferior. In Christ, he concludes, the whole penalty, as Paul teaches, has been abrogated, and the Christian woman is no more inferior to the man than is the Gentile to the Jew, or the bondman to the free.

17.pericope_label: Cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee

schools.summary: Henry prefaces the sentence with a recital of the crime: because thou hast hearkened to the voice of thy wife. Adam excused the fault by laying it on his wife, but God does not admit the excuse — she could but tempt him, she could not force him, and though it was her fault to persuade him to eat, it was his fault to hearken to her. Thus men's frivolous pleas will, in the day of God's judgment, not only be overruled but turned against them, and made the grounds of their sentence. Henry then puts three marks of displeasure upon Adam. First his habitation is cursed, and the effect of that curse is thorns and thistles; his dwelling is changed, so that he should no longer dwell in a distinguished, blessed paradise, but be removed to common ground, and that cursed. The ground is here put for the whole visible creation, which by the sin of man is made subject to vanity, its several parts being not so serviceable to man's comfort and happiness as they were designed to be. Fruitfulness was its blessing for man's service, and now barrenness is its curse for man's punishment; sin turned a fruitful land into barrenness. Yet there is a mixture of mercy: Adam himself is not cursed, as the serpent was, but only the ground for his sake, and he is yet above ground, the earth does not open and swallow him up but continues to be his habitation; and this curse upon the earth, cutting off all expectations of happiness in things below, might direct and quicken him to look for bliss only in things above. Secondly his employments and enjoyments are embittered. His business, which before he sinned was a constant pleasure to him, the garden being dressed without any uneasy labour, shall now become a toil, and he shall go on with it in the sweat of his face; if Adam had not sinned, he had not sweated. Labour is our duty, which we must faithfully perform, and we are bound to work not as creatures only but as criminals, it being part of our sentence, which idleness daringly defies; uneasiness and weariness with labour are our just punishment, which we must patiently submit to and not complain of, since they are less than our iniquity deserves. His food too is changed, both in matter and in manner: he must now eat the herb of the field and no longer be feasted with the delicacies of the garden, and he must eat it in sorrow. Yet here also mercy is mixed with wrath — he shall sweat, but his toil shall make his rest the more welcome; he shall grieve, but he shall not starve; he shall have sorrow, but in that sorrow he shall eat bread, which shall strengthen his heart under his sorrows; and he is not sentenced to eat dust as the serpent, only to eat the herb of the field.

Gill notes that Adam is addressed last of all, being the last that sinned, but not therefore to be excused; and of the thorns and thistles he says they were brought forth not for his advantage, but to give him more trouble and cause him more fatigue and sorrow to root them up. They include all sorts of noxious herbs and plants and troublesome weeds, which added to man's labour to pluck them up that those more useful might grow and flourish; and Rabbi Eliezer was of opinion that if there had not been a new blessing upon the earth it would have brought forth nothing else, as that which is rejected and nigh unto cursing does — a curse which continued, or at least was not wholly removed, until the times of Noah, and which made it hard and difficult for the antediluvian patriarchs to get their bread. Calvin begins by observing that the punishment was not inflicted upon the first of our race so as to rest on those two alone, but was extended generally to all their posterity, in order that we might know that the human race was cursed in their person; and that they were subjected only to temporal punishment, so that from the moderation of the divine anger they might entertain hope of pardon. By adducing the reason why he thus punishes the man, God cuts off from him the occasion of murmuring, for no excuse was left to him who had obeyed his wife rather than God — yea, had despised God for the sake of his wife, placing so much confidence in the fallacies of Satan that he did not hesitate perfidiously to deny his Maker. On the curse itself Calvin corrects the ancient interpreter, who translated it "in thy work," and retains the reading in which all the Hebrew copies agree, that the earth was cursed. As the blessing of the earth means, in the language of Scripture, that fertility which God infuses by his secret power, so the curse is nothing else than the opposite privation, when God withdraws his favour. Nor ought it to seem absurd that through the sin of man punishment should overflow the earth, though innocent; for as the outermost heaven was thought to roll all the celestial spheres along with it, so the ruin of man drives headlong all those creatures which were formed for his sake and had been made subject to him. Properly speaking, the whole punishment is exacted not from the earth itself but from man alone, for the earth does not bear fruit for itself. Before the fall the state of the world was a most fair and delightful mirror of the divine favour and paternal indulgence towards man; now, in all the elements, we perceive that we are cursed, and if we are unmoved by the manifest signs of his dreadful alienation from us we betray our blindness and insensibility. Yet, lest sadness and horror should overwhelm us, the Lord sprinkles everywhere the tokens of his goodness, so that David may truly and properly exclaim that the earth is full of the mercy of God. Of the labour Calvin adds that the word rendered sorrow stands in antithesis with the pleasant labour in which Adam previously so employed himself that in a sense he might be said to play; he was not formed for idleness but for action, and the Lord had placed him over a garden to be cultivated, but whereas in that labour there had been sweet delight, now servile work is enjoined upon him as if he were condemned to the mines — though the asperity of this punishment also is mitigated by the clemency of God, since something of enjoyment is blended with the labours of men.

Clarke puts the charge in the second person: thou wast not deceived, she only gave and counselled thee to eat, and this thou shouldst have resisted; and that he did not is the reason of his condemnation. From henceforth, he says, the fertility of the ground shall be greatly impaired, and in sorrow shalt thou eat of it means to be in continual perplexity concerning the seed time and the harvest, the cold and the heat, the wet and the dry — how often are all the fruits of man's toil destroyed by blasting, by mildew, by insects, wet weather, land floods; anxiety and carefulness are the labouring man's portion. On the thorns and thistles Clarke thinks much more is implied than generally appears, and demonstrates it by the amazing fertility of the most common thistles and thorns, which renders them the most proper instruments for the fulfilment of this sentence. He counts the heads and seeds of two species, reckons the increase through four successive years, and concludes that a single plant would furnish a progeny more than sufficient to stock not only the surface of the whole world but of all the planets of the solar system, so that no other vegetable could possibly grow. He notes too the hedge thistle, which besides the swarms of winged seeds it sends forth spreads its roots many yards and throws up suckers everywhere; and the furze, allowed to be one of the most mischievous shrubs on the face of the earth, so thick set with prickles that it is almost impossible to touch it without being wounded, and so prolific that where it is permitted to grow it soon overspreads whole tracts of ground. Instead of nourishing grain and useful vegetables, noxious weeds shall be peculiarly prolific, injure the ground, choke the good seed and mock the hopes of the husbandman; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field means that man shall no longer have the privilege of this garden of delights, but must go to the common champaign country and feed on such herbs as he can find, till by labour and industry he has raised others more suitable and more comfortable. Wesley abridges Henry: God does not admit the excuse, for though it was her fault to persuade him to eat it, it was his fault to hearken to her; and the ground or earth, by the sin of man, is made subject to vanity, the several parts of it being not so serviceable to man's comfort and happiness as they were when they were made, so that fruitfulness was its blessing for man's service, and now barrenness is its curse for man's punishment.

Keil and Delitzsch note first a point of grammar, that the noun is here used for the first time as a proper name without the article, whereas earlier in the narrative it had been appellative. The sentence upon Adam they find to include a twofold punishment: first the cursing of the ground, and secondly death, which affects the woman as well, on account of their common guilt. Each answers to a distinct element in the offence. By listening to the voice of his wife when she had been deceived by the serpent, Adam had repudiated his superiority to the rest of creation; as a punishment, therefore, nature would henceforth offer resistance to his will. By breaking the divine command, he had set himself above his Maker; death would therefore show him the worthlessness of his own nature. The clause "cursed be the ground for thy sake" they take with the following words as one sentence, the ground standing by synecdoche for what it yields, so that the eating in sorrow is of the produce of the cursed soil.

19.pericope_label: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return

schools.summary: Gill reads the sweat of the face literally and then widely. The Hebrew is of thy nose, sweat appearing first and chiefly on the forehead, from whence it trickles down by the nose in persons employed in hard labour; and the clause takes in all the labour used in cultivating the earth for the production of herbs, and particularly of corn, of which bread is made, with respect to which there are various operations in which men sweat — ploughing, sowing, reaping, threshing, winnowing, grinding, sifting, kneading and baking. It may have regard to all the methods and means by which men get their bread, and not without sweat; and even such exercises as depend upon the brain are not excused from the expense. So that every man, let him be in what station of life he will, is not exempt, more or less, from this sentence, and so continues till he dies. Calvin is chiefly concerned to prevent the verse being made into a rule. Some translate the word labour, which he thinks forced; by sweat is understood hard labour, full of fatigue and weariness, which by its difficulty produces sweat, and the clause is a repetition of the former sentence. Under cover of this passage, he says, certain ignorant persons would rashly impel all men to manual labour; but God is not here teaching as a master or legislator, he is only denouncing punishment as a judge. If a rule had been prescribed here, it would be necessary for all to become husbandmen, nor would any place be given to the mechanical arts, and we must go out of the world to seek clothing and the other necessary conveniences of life.
