What the passage means is that God pronounces, as from his judgment-seat, that the life of man shall henceforth be miserable, because Adam had proved himself unworthy of that tranquil, happy and joyful state for which he had been created. Should any object that there are many inactive and indolent persons, this does not prevent the curse from having spread over the whole human race, for no one lies torpid in such a degree of sloth as not to be under the necessity of experiencing that this curse belongs to all: some flee from troubles, and many more do all they can to grasp at immunity from them, but the Lord subjects all, without exception, to this yoke of imposed servitude. It is nevertheless to be maintained that labour is not imposed equally on each, but on some more and on others less, so that what is described here is the labour common to the whole body, not that which belongs peculiarly to each member. Those who meekly submit to their sufferings present to God an acceptable obedience, if there be joined with the bearing of the cross that knowledge of sin which teaches them to be humble; the faithful, the more they labour in procuring a livelihood, are with the greater advantage stimulated to repentance and accustomed to the mortification of the flesh. Yet God often remits a portion of this curse to his own children, lest they should sink beneath the burden, and to that purpose Calvin cites the Psalm which says that some will rise early and go late to rest and eat the bread of carefulness, but the Lord will give to his beloved sleep. Of the death itself he says that God denounces that the termination of a miserable life shall be death, as if he would say that Adam should at length come, through various and continued kinds of evil, to the last evil of all; the death of Adam had commenced immediately from the day of his transgression, for this accursed life of man could be nothing else than the beginning of death. And as soon as he had been raised to a dignity so great that the glory of the Divine Image shone in him, the terrestrial origin of his body was almost obliterated; now, however, after he had been despoiled of his divine and heavenly excellence, what remains but that by his very departure out of life he should recognise himself to be earth? Hence it is that we dread death, because dissolution, which is contrary to nature, cannot naturally be desired.

Clarke explains the physiology of the sweat and then turns it into a memorial. Though the whole body may be thrown into a profuse sweat if hard labour be long continued, yet the face or forehead is the first part whence the sweat begins to issue; this is occasioned by the blood being strongly propelled to the brain, partly through stooping but principally by the strong action of the muscles, in consequence of which the blood vessels about the head become turgid, the fibres are relaxed, the pores enlarged, and the sweat poured out. Thus, then, the very commencement of every man's labour may put him in mind of his sin and its consequences. On the return to dust Clarke recalls the original threatening, that in the day they ate of the forbidden fruit, dying they should die: they should then become mortal, and continue under the influence of a great variety of unfriendly agencies in the atmosphere and in themselves — heats, colds, drought and damps without, and morbid increased and decreased action in the solids and fluids within — till the spirit, finding its earthly house no longer tenable, should return to God who gave it, and the body, being decomposed, should be reduced to its primitive dust. It is evident from this, he argues, that man would have been immortal had he never transgressed, and that this state of continual life and health depended on his obedience to his Maker; the tree of life was intended to be the means of continual preservation, for as no being but God can exist independently of any supporting agency, so man could not have continued to live without a particular supporting agent. Wesley marks the change in the labour and the end of the body: his business before he sinned was a constant pleasure to him, but now his labour shall be a weariness; and unto dust shalt thou return means that his body shall be forsaken by his soul, and become itself a lump of dust, and then be lodged in the grave and mingle with the dust of the earth.

Ellicott takes the clause as evidence that mortality belonged to the body's own constitution. A spiritual being is eternal by its own constitution, but the argument by which Bishop Butler proves the soul to be immortal equally proves the mortality of the body: death, he says, is the division of a compound substance into its component parts, and as the soul is a simple substance, and incapable of division, it is in itself incapable of death. The body of Adam, composed of particles of earth, was capable of division, and our first parents in Paradise were assured of an unending existence by a special gift, typified by the tree of life; but now this gift was withdrawn, and henceforward the sweat of man's brow was in itself proof that he was returning to his earth, for it told of exhaustion and waste. Ellicott adds a judgment on labour itself. Even now labour is a blessing only when it is moderate, as when Adam kept a garden that spontaneously brought forth flowers and fruit; in excess it wears out the body and benumbs the soul, and by the pressure of earthly cares leaves neither time nor the wish for any such pursuits as are worthy of a being endowed with thought and reason and a soul.

20.pericope_label: Adam called his wife’s name Eve, because she was the mother of all living; and the LORD God made coats of skins, and clothed them

schools.summary: Henry sets the two names side by side. God having named the man and called him Adam, which signifies red earth, Adam, in further token of dominion, named the woman and called her Eve, that is, life; Adam bears the name of the dying body, Eve that of the living soul. He had before called her woman, as a wife; here he calls her life, as a mother. The reason of the name is given in the text — because she was, that is, was to be, the mother of all living — and Henry offers two readings of the act. If it was done by divine direction, it was an instance of God's favour, and, like the new naming of Abraham and Sarah, it was a seal of the covenant and an assurance to them that, notwithstanding their sin and his displeasure against them for it, he had not reversed the blessing wherewith he had blessed them, to be fruitful and multiply; and it was likewise a confirmation of the promise just made, that the seed of the woman should break the serpent's head. If Adam did it of himself, it was an instance of his faith in the word of God — not, as some have suspected, in contempt or defiance of the curse, but rather in a humble confidence and dependence upon the blessing: the blessing of a reprieve, admiring the patience of God that he should spare such sinners to be the parents of all living; and the blessing of a Redeemer, the promised seed, to whom Adam had an eye in calling his wife life, for he should be the life of all the living, and in him all the families of the earth should be blessed. Of the clothing Henry finds a further instance of God's care notwithstanding their sin: though he corrects his disobedient children and puts them under the marks of his displeasure, yet he does not disinherit them, but like a tender father provides the herb of the field for their food and coats of skins for their clothing; if the Lord had been pleased to kill them, he would not have done this for them. He draws four observations. Clothes came in with sin, and we should have had no occasion for them, either for defence or decency, if sin had not made us naked to our shame, so that little reason have we to be proud of our clothes, which are but the badges of our poverty and infamy. When God made clothes for our first parents he made them warm and strong, but coarse and very plain, not robes of scarlet but coats of skin, so let the poor that are meanly clad learn not to complain, and let the rich that are finely clad learn not to make the putting on of apparel their adorning. God is to be acknowledged with thankfulness not only in giving us food but in giving us clothes also. And these coats of skin had a significancy: the beasts whose skins they were must be slain, slain before their eyes, to show them what death is, and it is supposed that they were slain not for food but for sacrifice, to typify the great sacrifice which in the latter end of the world should be offered once for all; so the first thing that died was a sacrifice, or Christ in a figure. The sacrifices were divided between God and man in token of reconciliation, the flesh offered to God and the skins given to man for clothing, signifying that we are to clothe ourselves with the righteousness of Christ as with a garment; for the aprons of fig-leaves were a covering too narrow to wrap themselves in, and such are all the rags of our own righteousness, but the coats of skin were large, strong, durable and fit for them.

Gill traces the name and its afterlife. She had before been named woman, because taken from the man, and now Adam gives her a new name upon this scene of things; it is derived not from the verb to show forth or declare, as if she were so called because she was loquacious and talkative, telling everything she knew, as some Jewish writers have it, but from the verb to live, as the reason given in the text shows. Gill notes that the word Eve is retained in many heathen writers, and used to be frequently repeated in the Bacchanalian rites, when the idolaters appeared with serpents platted on their heads, which plainly refers to the affair between the serpent and Eve, and that hence Bacchus is sometimes called Evius. Of the clothing he observes that besides the kind intimation of grace and favour to them, another token of God's good will was shown in this, that whereas they were naked and ashamed, he covered them. Calvin allows two ways of reading the naming. Taken as a pluperfect, the sense would be that Adam had been greatly deceived in promising to himself and his posterity so much from a wife whom he afterwards found by experience to be the introducer of death. Taken otherwise, it may be understood in a good or a bad sense: some think that Adam, animated by the hope of a happier condition, because God had promised that the head of the serpent should be wounded by the seed of the woman, called her by a name implying life, which would be a noble and even heroic fortitude of mind; but Calvin fears the conjecture is weak, and asks the reader to consider whether Moses did not design rather to tax Adam with thoughtlessness, who, being himself immersed in death, yet gave to his wife so proud a name. He does not doubt that when Adam heard the declaration of God concerning the prolongation of life he began again to breathe and to take courage, and then, as one revived, gave his wife a name derived from life; but it does not follow that by a faith accordant with the word of God he triumphed, as he ought to have done, over death. On the garments Calvin cautions that it is not proper to understand the words as if God had been a furrier, or a servant to sew clothes; the skins were not presented by chance, but the pair, impelled by a new necessity, put animals to death in order to cover themselves, having been divinely directed to that counsel, and therefore Moses calls God its author. The reason for skins he takes to be that garments formed of such material would have a more degrading appearance than those made of linen or of woollen, so that in such a dress our first parents should behold their own vileness, just as they had before seen it in their nudity, and should thus be reminded of their sin. He adds that God would also propose an example by which to accustom us to a frugal and inexpensive mode of dress, not that every kind of ornament is to be expressly condemned, but because when immoderate elegance and splendour is carefully sought after, that Master is despised who intended clothing to be a sign of shame.

Clarke complains that a reader without the original cannot possibly comprehend the reason given here: what has the word Eve to do with being the mother of all living? Our translators often follow the Septuagint, and it is a pity they had not done so here, since the Septuagint translation is literal and correct — Adam called his wife's name Life, because she was the mother of all the living. The Hebrew Chavvah, which we have corrupted into Eve, a word destitute of all meaning, answers exactly to the Greek, both signifying life. Clarke thinks God designed by this name to teach our first parents two important truths: that though they had merited immediate death, yet they should be respited, and the accomplishment of the sentence long delayed, so that they should be spared to propagate a numerous progeny on the earth; and that though much misery would be entailed on his posterity, and death should have a long and universal empire, yet One should in the fullness of time spring from the woman, who should destroy death and bring life and immortality to light. On the coats of skins he thinks it very likely that the skins were taken off animals whose blood had been poured out as a sin-offering to God, since we find Cain and Abel afterwards offering sacrifices, and may fairly presume that God had given instructions on this head; nor is it likely that the notion of a sacrifice could ever have occurred to the mind of man without an express revelation. As Adam and Eve needed this clothing as soon as they fell, and death had not as yet made any ravages in the animal world, it is most likely that the skins were taken off victims offered under the direction of God himself, and in faith of him who in the fullness of time was to make an atonement by his death; and it seems reasonable that the matter should be brought about in such a way that Satan and death should have no triumph, the very first death that took place in the world being an emblem and type of that death which should conquer Satan and reconcile God to man. Wesley keeps Henry's two readings of the name, and his account of the significancy of the skins: the beasts whose skins they were must be slain, slain before their eyes, to show them what death is, and probably slain for sacrifice, to typify the great sacrifice which in the latter end of the world should be offered once for all, so that the first thing that died was a sacrifice, or Christ in a figure.

Ellicott debates whether the name is a substantive, Life, as the Septuagint took it, or a participle, Life-producer, as Symmachus had it, and then draws out the situation which the naming reveals. Adam's condition was now one of death, but his wife thereby attained a higher value in his sight, since through her alone could human life be continued, and the woman's seed be obtained who was to raise up man from his fall. While, then, woman's punishment consists in the multiplication of her sorrow and conception, she becomes thereby only more precious to man; and while her desire is to her husband, Adam turns from his own punishment to look upon her with more tender love. He has no word for her of reproach, from which Ellicott concludes that the common interpretation of Adam's earlier answer is more than doubtful: Adam throws no blame either on Eve or on his Maker, because he does not feel himself to blame, and rather means, how could I err in following one so noble, and in whom I recognise Thy best and choicest gift? And so here he turns to her and calls her his life, his compensation for his loss, and the antidote for the sentence of death. Of the coats of skins he infers that animals were therefore killed even in Paradise, and that until sin entered the world no sacrifices could have been offered; if, therefore, these were the skins of animals offered in sacrifice, as many suppose, Adam must in some way, immediately after the fall, have been taught that without shedding of blood is no remission of sin, but that God will accept a vicarious sacrifice. This he takes to be perhaps the most tenable view. It shows also that the innocence of our first parents was gone: in his happy state Adam had studied the animals, tamed them and made them his friends, and now a sense of guilt urges him to inflict upon them pain and suffering and death. But in the first sacrifice was laid the foundation of the whole Mosaical dispensation, and man went forth equipped with raiment suited for the harder lot that awaited him, and, better far, with peace for his soul and the thought, even if still faint and dim, of the possibility of an atonement. Keil and Delitzsch read the naming as an act of faith, and set it in the order of justice and mercy: justice in that God cursed the tempter alone, and only punished the tempted with labour and mortality; mercy in the promise of eventual triumph over the serpent. God displayed his mercy to the fallen before carrying the sentence into effect, and it was through the power of divine grace that Adam believed the promise with regard to the woman's seed, and manifested his faith in the name which he gave to his wife — an old form of the word signifying life, or life-spring, and a substantive rather than a feminine adjective meaning the living one.

22.pericope_label: Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil; and the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground

schools.summary: Gill notes that the speaker is the Word of the Lord God, as the Jerusalem Targum has it, and that the words are not addressed to ministering angels, as the Targum of Jonathan supposed, but spoken within himself, or to the other two divine Persons. Of the expulsion he says that God gave Adam orders to depart immediately, sending or putting him away as a man does his wife when he divorces her, or as a prince banishes a rebellious subject; yet he did not send him to hell at once, as he did the apostate angels. Calvin takes the saying as an ironical reproof by which God would not only prick the heart of man, but pierce it through and through. He does not, however, cruelly triumph over the miserable and afflicted, but, according to the necessity of the disease, applies a more violent remedy; for though Adam was confounded and astonished at his calamity, he did not so deeply reflect on its cause as to become weary of his pride and learn to embrace true humility. God inveighed by this irony not more against Adam himself than against his posterity, for the purpose of commending modesty to all ages. And truly it was a sad and horrid spectacle, that he in whom the glory of the Divine image had recently been shining should lie hidden under fetid skins to cover his own disgrace, and that there should be more comeliness in a dead animal than in a living man. The clause about knowing good and evil describes the cause of so great misery, namely that Adam, not content with his condition, had tried to ascend higher than was lawful; as if it had been said, see now whither thy ambition and thy perverse appetite for illicit knowledge have precipitated thee. Yet the Lord does not even deign to hold converse with him, but contemptuously draws him forth, for the sake of exposing him to greater infamy; thus was it necessary for his iron pride to be beaten down, that he might at length descend into himself. On the plural Calvin declines the common Christian argument, thinking the passage not sufficiently firm for the doctrine of the three Persons, since here Adam is included in the word Us, whereas in the earlier "let us make man" a distinction in the essence of God is expressed. Of the tree of life he supplies the defective sentence — it now remains that in future he be debarred from the fruit of the tree of life — and denies that this too is irony, as if God were saying the tree would not have profited him; rather, by depriving him of the symbol he takes away also the thing signified. The tree was given as a pledge of life, and so a solemn excommunication is added, not that the Lord would cut him off from all hope of salvation, but that by taking away what he had given he might cause man to seek new assistance elsewhere; there remained an expiation in sacrifices, which might restore him to the life he had lost, and from the moment he became alienated from God it was necessary that he should recover life by the death of Christ. At the expulsion itself Calvin finds mercy again: God softens the exile of Adam by still providing for him a remaining home on earth, and by assigning to him a livelihood from the culture — although the laborious culture — of the ground, whence Adam infers that the Lord has some care for him, which is a proof of paternal love. He was banished from that royal palace of which he had been the lord, but he obtained elsewhere a place in which he might dwell; he was bereft of his former delicacies, yet he was still supplied with some kind of food; he was excommunicated from the tree of life, but a new remedy was offered him in sacrifices.

Henry treats the verses as execution following sentence, and observes first how they were justly disgraced and shamed before God and the holy angels by the ironical upbraiding of them with the issue of their enterprise: behold, the man has become as one of us, to know good and evil — a goodly god he makes, does he not; see what he has got, what preferments, what advantages, by eating forbidden fruit. This was said to awaken and humble them, and to bring them to a sense of their sin and folly and to repentance for it, that, seeing themselves thus wretchedly deceived by following the devil's counsel, they might henceforth pursue the happiness God should offer in the way he should prescribe. God thus fills their faces with shame, that they may seek his name, and puts them to this confusion in order to their conversion; true penitents will upbraid themselves the same way, asking what fruit they now have by sin. Then he shows how they were justly discarded and shut out of paradise. The reason given is not only that he had put forth his hand and taken of the tree of knowledge, which was his sin, but lest he should again put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, now forbidden him by the divine sentence, and should dare to eat of that tree, and so profane a divine sacrament and defy a divine sentence, and yet flatter himself with a conceit that thereby he should live for ever. Henry draws two notes from this. There is a foolish proneness in those that have rendered themselves unworthy of the substance of Christian privileges to catch at the signs and shadows of them, and many that like not the terms of the covenant are yet, for their reputation's sake, fond of the seals of it. And it is not only justice but kindness to such to be denied them, for by usurping that to which they have no title they affront God and make their sin the more heinous, and by building their hopes upon a wrong foundation they render their conversion the more difficult and their ruin the more deplorable. Of the manner of the expulsion Henry notes that God bade him go out, told him that that was no place for him, but he liked the place too well to be willing to part with it, and therefore God drove him out, made him go out whether he would or no; this signified the exclusion of him and all his guilty race from that communion with God which was the bliss and glory of paradise. Yet Henry marks how far the sentence stops short: God might justly have chased him out of the world, but he only chased him out of the garden; he might justly have cast him down to hell, as he did the angels that sinned, but man was only sent to till the ground out of which he was taken. He was sent to a place of toil, not to a place of torment; to the ground, not to the grave; to the work-house, not to the dungeon; to hold the plough, not to drag the chain. His tilling the ground would be recompensed by his eating of its fruits, and his converse with the earth whence he was taken was improvable to good purposes, to keep him humble and to remind him of his latter end. Though our first parents were excluded from the privileges of their state of innocency, they were not abandoned to despair, God's thoughts of love designing them for a second state of probation upon new terms.

Clarke says that on all hands this text is allowed to be difficult, and that the difficulty is increased by our translation, which is opposed to the original Hebrew and the most authentic versions. The Hebrew verb is the third person preterite and signifies was, not is, and the Samaritan text, the Samaritan version, the Syriac and the Septuagint all have the same tense. These lead to a very different sense, and indicate an ellipsis of some words which must be supplied to make the sense complete; and Clarke commends the paraphrase of a very learned man: the man who was like one of us in purity and wisdom is now fallen and robbed of his excellence; he has added, to the knowledge of the good, by his transgression the knowledge of the evil; and now, lest he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, and eat and live for ever in this miserable state, I will remove him, and guard the place lest he should re-enter. This seems to him the most natural sense of the place. Some suppose that the removal from the tree of life was in mercy, to prevent a second temptation, since Adam had already imagined that he could gain an increase of wisdom by eating of the tree of knowledge, and Satan would be disposed to tempt him to elude the sentence of death by eating of the tree of life. Others imagine that the words are spoken ironically, and that the Most High intended by a cutting taunt to upbraid the poor culprit for his offence; but Clarke rejects this, because God is ever consistent with himself, and surely his infinite pity prohibited the use of either sarcasm or irony in speaking of so dreadful a catastrophe, that was in the end to occasion the agony and bloody sweat, the cross and passion, the death and burial of Him in whom dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. He closes with a comparison: earlier in the book we have seen man in the perfection of his nature, the dignity of his office and the plenitude of his happiness, and here we find the same creature, but stripped of his glories, so that the word man no longer conveys the same ideas it did before — man and intellectual excellence were before so intimately connected as to appear inseparable, and man and misery are now equally so. Wesley keeps the reproof brief: see what he has got, what advantages, by eating forbidden fruit; this is said to humble them, and to bring them to a sense of their sin and folly, that seeing themselves thus wretchedly deceived by following the devil's counsel, they might henceforth pursue the happiness God offers, in the way he prescribes.

Keil and Delitzsch deny the irony flatly. Clothed in the sign of mercy, the man was driven out of paradise to bear the punishment of his sin; and the words of Jehovah, the man is become as one of Us to know good and evil, contain no irony, as though man had exalted himself to a position of autonomy resembling that of God — for irony at the expense of a wretched tempted soul might well befit Satan, but not the Lord. Likeness to God is predicated only with regard to the knowledge of good and evil, in which the man really had become like God. The purpose of the exclusion follows from the state he was now in: since the germ of death had penetrated into his nature along with sin, he must not take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever. Ellicott agrees that there is something painful and humiliating in the idea of Chrysostom and other Fathers that the Deity was speaking ironically, or even, as Augustine had it, with insult. All those qualities which constitute man's likeness to God — free-will, self-dependence, the exercise of reason and of choice — had been developed by the fall, and Adam was now a very different being from what he had been in the days of his simple innocency. Adam had exercised the power of marring God's work, and if an unending physical life were added to the gift of free-will now in revolt against God, his condition and that of mankind would become most miserable. Man is still to attain to immortality, but it must now be through struggle, sorrow, penitence, faith and death; hence a paradise is no fit home for him, and the Divine mercy therefore commands Adam to quit it, in order that he may live under conditions better suited for his moral and spiritual good. Ellicott adds a note on the task assigned him outside: to till the ground is the same word rendered dress in the earlier chapter, so that Adam's task is the same, but the conditions are altered.

24.pericope_label: So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life

schools.summary: Clarke notes three things in the driving out: God's displeasure against sinful man, evidenced by his expelling him from this place of blessedness; man's unfitness for the place, of which he had rendered himself unworthy by his ingratitude and transgression; and his reluctance to leave this place of happiness, since he was unwilling to depart, and God drove him out. On the guards he first corrects the English word, since Hebrew plurals in the masculine end in im, and to add an s when we introduce such words into English is very improper: the word should be written cherubim. But what were these? They are utterly unknown, he says, and conjectures and guesses relative to their nature and properties are endless. Several think them emblematical representations of the sacred Trinity and bring reasons and scriptures in support, but he is not satisfied that the opinion is correct. From the descriptions of the tabernacle and temple it appears that the cherubs were sometimes represented with two faces, those of a lion and of a man, while in Ezekiel they have four faces and four wings — a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle — with but one body to these heads; the two-faced cherubs were those represented on the curtains and veil of the tabernacle and on the wall, doors and veil of the temple, while those with four faces appeared only in the holy of holies. Since the word never appears as a verb in the Hebrew Bible, he takes it to be compounded of a particle of resemblance and a root meaning he was great or powerful, and so concludes that the cherubim, to whatever order of beings they belonged, were emblems of the Almighty, and were those creatures by whom he produced the great effects of his power. These angelic beings were for a time employed in guarding the entrance to Paradise and keeping the way of the tree of life — for a time, he says, since it is very probable that God soon removed the tree of life and abolished the garden, so that its situation could never after be positively ascertained. By the flaming sword turning every way, or the flame folding back upon itself, we may understand the formidable appearances which these cherubim assumed, in order to render the passage to the tree of life inaccessible. Clarke closes the chapter as a tragedy in which all the actors are slain: the serpent degraded, the woman cursed with pains and miseries and a subjection which was never originally designed, the man doomed to incessant labour and toil, the earth itself cursed with comparative barrenness, the garden of pleasure interdicted, and this man, who was made after the image of God, shamefully expelled. Yet in the midst of wrath God remembers mercy, and a promise of redemption from this degraded and cursed state is made to them through Him who, in the fullness of time, is to be made flesh, and who by dying for the sin of the world shall destroy the power of Satan. He adds a reflection on death itself: sin, growing with the growth of man, would be endless in its duration and unlimited in its influence did not God check and restrain it by his grace, and cut off its extending influence in the incorrigibly wicked by means of death; so that which entered into the world as one of the prime fruits of sin is now an instrument in his hands to prevent the extension of its contagion. And on the barred way he remarks that for some thousands of years men have laboured to find means to prevent death, and that their own deaths, in the common order of nature, are a continual proof that the cherubim, with their flaming swords, are turning every way to keep the passage of the tree of life. Wesley, keeping close to Henry, reads the driving out as signifying the exclusion of Adam and his guilty race from that communion with God which was the bliss and glory of paradise, and describes the guard as a detachment of cherubim armed with a dreadful and irresistible power, represented by flaming swords which turned every way, posted on that side of the garden which lay next to the place whither Adam was sent, to keep the way that led to the tree of life.

Ellicott says the verb implies displeasure and compulsion: Adam departed unwillingly from his happy home, and with the consciousness that he had incurred the Divine anger; it was the consequence of his sin, and was a punishment, even if necessary for his good under the changed circumstances produced by his disobedience. The word rendered "he placed" is literally "caused to dwell," and the return to Paradise was closed for ever; yet Adam still had his habitation in the land of Eden, and probably in the immediate neighbourhood of Paradise. Of the cherub Ellicott says it was a symbolical figure, representing strength and majesty. The ordinary derivation, from a root signifying to carve, grave, and especially to plough, compared with the description of the mercy-seat, suggests to him that the cherubim were winged bulls, probably with human heads, like those brought from Nineveh. He warns expressly that we must not confound them with the four living creatures of Ezekiel's vision, which are the beasts of the Revelation of John, and which have a far different office and signification. The office of the cherub here is to guard the Paradise, lest man should try to force an entrance back; and so too the office of the cherubs upon the mercy-seat was to protect it, lest any one should impiously approach it, except the high-priest on the Day of Atonement.

Gill finds in the verb the language of divorce. Adam being unwilling to go out upon the orders given, some degree of force was used, or power exerted in some way, to oblige him to depart; and the word by which it is expressed is used of divorces. There was a conjugal relation between God and man, Gill argues, the covenant between them having the nature of a matrimonial contract; which covenant man broke, though God was a husband to him, by committing idolatry, that is spiritual adultery, in not giving credit to him but believing the devil before him. Wherefore God wrote him a bill of divorce and sent him away, driving him from his presence and communion with him, from his house and habitation, from his seat of pleasure and garden of delight, and from all the comfortable enjoyments of life — an emblem of that separation and distance which sin makes between God and his creature, and of the loss which is sustained thereby. He notes also the Septuagint reading, which turns the clause about, making God cause Adam to dwell over against the paradise of pleasure, and then order the cherubim; but Gill does not think the words are to be so taken.
